chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
title: Charlie Parker in Kansas City and New York; Tate tries to get him into Basie's band
summary: Tate knew Parker as a student of Buster Smith in 1934 and later tried to place him with Basie.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Okay, now, it's 1939, you're with Basie.
And you just married the third time.
'36. Were you aware of Bird yet?

1934. See, I was with -- I knew him when he was taking lessons from Buster Smith. That's why I know that's authentic, you know, like he always dug Prof and see, Prof used to play like that, although Bird went farther. But that was basically Buster Smith's style. He played like that, alto and soft and runs like Bird. Bird went further, as I say. But that was his idol, was Buster Smith, and he was trying to learn how to play then in '33 and '34.
Was there anything special about him then?
So it was kind of a surprise when --

Yeah, it really was kind of a surprise. I tried to get him in Basie's band, though. When we come to New York in '39, he really hadn't made it, you know. And he was staying uptown, sleeping up to Monroe's place uptown, Monroe's uptown house, that's where we used to go all the time. And he was like sleeping in the basement up there. And he always wanted to be with the band because he felt like being from Kansas City, he should have been, you know. And of course, at the time, we didn't have but four saxaphone and Basie would always tell me, "Yes, I'll think about it." But he was really putting me off, you know. I -- and then I remember he told me one time, he says, he didn't look right, you know, he looked too bad, you know.
You know, his appearance, you know. I says, "You've got a lot of cats in the band would look bad if you didn't put those uniforms on them."

But still, I didn't ever get him. He didn't ever forget that. He always remembered me trying to get him in the band. And I used to have my wife -- I used to tell him to come up to the house. We didn't call, you know, like our cooking "soul food" then. We called it "down home," you know. I say, "Come on up to the house and I'll fix you a down home meal. And I'll have my wife to do it." So he says, "Okay." I says, "What do you want?" He says, "Well, you know what I like, anything." So he would come up there, this apartment I got now, and he'd come up and she'd fix him -- he's take only a few bites, next thing I knew, he was asleep. But I didn't know what was happening then, you know, he would be -- you know, he'd start to dozing. I think he must have been kind of on his way then, you know.
